en: v1.3 — Placing nikkud & trop now works like the rest of the tool: your moves apply live and you can leave a letter freely — no save dialog — with undo as the safety net. The grid now tells confirmed placements apart from ones carried over from the previous letter: a solid green ✓ means you reviewed it, a hollow amber ✓ means "carried over — review & confirm", and amber ! means unconfirmed. "Save Placement" is now an optional ✓ Confirm placement review marker. The step tabs show a per-letter checklist (✓ done / ✗ to-do / – not needed) for the letter you're on. The toolbar is now grouped — Project · History · Review · Export — with Export the clear primary action and Help moved up to the top corner. (June 2026)

v1.4 — A new Edit shape editor lets you redesign any nikkud, dagesh, or trop mark from simple dots and bars — round or square dots, square or rounded bars — then apply your shape to the current letter or to all letters. Position each dot or bar by dragging it, nudging with the arrow keys, or typing exact X / Y coordinates — and set a dot's radius or a bar's width & height — for pixel-perfect placement; Reset restores a mark's default shape, and undo / redo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z) covers every change in the editor. The on-stage selection box hugs the mark's actual shape so a small or square mark is never hidden under the handle. (June 2026)

v1.5 — Trop marks can now sit Left, Center, or Right of a letter, not just above or below — so each cantillation mark lands on the correct part of the glyph and look-alikes (e.g. Yetiv vs. Mahpakh, Geresh vs. Geresh Muqdam) read correctly. Every mark has a sensible default side (Segol, Zarqa, Pashta & Telisha Qetana go left; Geresh Muqdam, Deḥi, Yetiv & Telisha Gedola go right; the rest stay centered) that you can change per mark in Place Trop, with a Default spread slider for how far the side marks shift. Need a custom position on one letter? Just drag the mark (or type exact X / Y) to override that letter alone. (June 2026)

v1.6 — New tools for spotting stacked-mark clashes. A Two marks tab in the Quality-check pairs any mark you pick (e.g. dagesh) with every other mark on every letter and flags where they overlap — handy for Babylonian pointing (vowels, dagesh & raphe all sit above) and two-vowel letters like יְרוּשָׁלִַם; the Stacked tab now also flags a vowel that collides with its trop. While placing nikkud you can preview a 2nd mark on the current letter and get a live overlap warning. Raphe now appears in the above-letter picker. (June 2026)

en: v1.7 — Drawing aids for consistency. New guides: drop adjustable horizontal & vertical lines on the canvas — drag them or type an exact position — that stay put across every letter, perfect for matching stroke thicknesses & heights. Copy outline from another letter seeds the current letter from one you've already drawn (copy Tav, delete the toe → Het, He, Resh), then reshape with ✎ Edit points. And the built-in ḥataf-patach & ḥataf-kamatz now have their sh'va dots aligned. (June 2026)

v1.8 — Kerning is easier to dial in. The big sample preview now updates live as you drag a pair's gap or add/remove pairs — not just the little two-glyph preview — so you see the effect in real words. The pair list now flags anything that won't export — ⚠ untraced glyphs or pairs still at 0 — with an "N of M pairs will be exported" summary, and highlights the pair you're editing. A reading-order hint clarifies that in Hebrew the first letter sits on the right, and class sides (Finals / Descenders) now show what they cover. (June 2026)

v1.9 — More kerning power. Suggest pairs now proposes an even starting gap — set by a new Auto-tightness slider — instead of seeding zeros, so one click gets you most of the way — measured optically from the real outlines (with the correct RTL facing edges), so overhanging letters like ר & ד tuck under the next one. And you can define your own kern classes: reusable named letter groups (alongside the built-in Finals & Descenders) that you kern as a unit on either side of a pair — edit a class and every pair using it updates. (June 2026)

en: v2.0 — A friendlier way in. A new Take a tour walkthrough spotlights each step right on your own workspace — start it from the welcome screen, the Help header, or Getting Started. The Export button now warms the font engine in the background as soon as you trace your first letter, so your first export is quick, and it shows what it's doing while it gets ready. When something's missing, the export warnings became clickable — tap a letter to jump straight to it — and a live “what's next?” line under the letters always points you to the next thing to do. Finally, press ? anytime for a keyboard-shortcut cheat sheet. (July 2026)

v2.1 — Custom glyphs are easier to size. The Width & margins controls now follow a letter through the Trace and Edit points steps — not just Align — so you can adjust a traced or duplicated glyph's spacing whenever you're working on its shape. Custom marks (which attach to a letter and have no width of their own) gained a Convert to main glyph button: turn a standalone symbol you built as a mark into a full glyph with its own adjustable width. And a hand-set width of zero is now respected instead of snapping back to the default. (July 2026)

v2.2 — Wide letters, Yiddish forms & custom glyphs got a big reliability pass. Nikkud and trop now attach correctly to wide letterforms and digraphs in the exported font (they used to slide to the left edge), wide forms export with smooth curves instead of chunky outlines, and a digraph's width no longer double-counts your letter spacing. The Specialized / Yiddish / Ladino tiles now show a live preview built from your own letters — including the Width slider's stretch — and clicking a form whose base isn't traced yet jumps you straight to tracing it. The Quality check now covers custom glyphs and custom marks, custom glyphs can be picked in kerning and added to the spacing sample with one click, and a custom glyph at a form's code point is protected from being overwritten at export (with a clear note on the tile). Export also warns if custom glyphs are blank or the custom-glyphs toggle is off. (July 2026)

v2.3 — Trop placement is safer and finer-grained. The Default spread slider no longer wipes out your hand-tuned Left/Right positions — letters you've adjusted keep their spots (with a note showing how many, and a Reset all side positions button when you really want a clean slate). A spread of 0 now sticks everywhere instead of quietly snapping back to the default. Every trop layout change — the spread, a mark's Left / Center / Right switch, and the new per-mark Height nudge — is now fully undoable (Ctrl/Cmd+Z). That Height row lets you raise or lower one trop mark on every letter, so two marks sharing a side (like Pashta and Telisha Qetana) no longer collide. And Check stacking now works while placing trop, too — preview a vowel in grey and get an instant overlap warning. (July 2026)

v2.4 — Wide letterforms & digraphs: the margin bands and width line on the canvas now outline the composed form — not its base letter — so they sit at the real edges of a digraph and follow the Width slider live as you stretch. (July 2026)

v2.5 — Stretching a wide letterform no longer runs it off the edge of the canvas — the workspace now widens to fit the whole composed glyph (and its right margin) at any Width, right up to 250%. (July 2026)

v2.6 — The Place Nikkud step for a wide letterform now makes sense: it previews the vowel right on the stretched form (where it will actually sit) and gives you a one-click “Edit nikkud on …” jump to the base letter, since a wide form's vowels follow the base — no more empty screen or a “drag the handle” hint with nothing to drag. (July 2026)

v2.7 — The mark size sliders are now undoable (Ctrl/Cmd+Z). Resizing the Nikkud, Holam, Dagesh, Holam (vav), or Trop marks and changing your mind now puts them right back — one undo step per slider drag, just like every other placement change. (July 2026)

v2.8 — The Place Nikkud / Trop step is tidier and works the way you'd expect. A letter's placement controls — the size sliders and the ✓ Confirm placement / Reset buttons — are now grouped right below the canvas (which fills the width), so nothing's stranded in a far-off strip. The above-mark picker now only offers marks that fit the letter (the shin/sin dots show up only on Shin), and picking any mark — Holam, Shin dot, Sin dot, or Rafe — now actually previews it on the canvas (Rafe used to do nothing). (July 2026)

v2.9 — The Place Nikkud / Trop panel now says what each control affects. Sections are grouped by scope — “Qamats — every letter” for a vowel's Height & shape, “Below position — Alef only” for this letter's X / Y — with a short plain-language line under each, replacing one long confusing paragraph. The size sliders under the canvas now sit side-by-side with dividers, so they take one tidy row instead of a stack. (July 2026)

v3.0 — Placement panel, take two: the size sliders under the canvas are stacked again (one per line, so each is easy to read), and the ✓ Confirm placement / Reset letter / Reset all buttons now sit together in their own panel to the right of the sliders instead of underneath them. (July 2026)

v3.1 — Four fixes. The shin/sin dots are now edited in just one place — Special & precomposed forms (שׁ/שׂ) — instead of also appearing in the above-mark row. Tracing no longer clips your letter at an invisible box: it follows your whole reference image, so a wide letter's edges and feet come through. Reopening a saved project now shows honest letter status — untraced letters no longer look finished — and your chosen reference (tracing) font is kept when you reload. (July 2026)

en: v3.2 — Undo now covers two more actions: showing/hiding guides and ✓ Confirm placement. Ctrl+Z steps back through both, just like every other edit. (July 2026)

v3.3 — Small correctness fix: nikkud and trop previews now center properly on a letter whose width is set to exactly zero (a rare edge case that previously fell back to the default width). (July 2026)
v3.4 — "Apply outline to all letters" now asks before overwriting each letter's own outline and line-weight settings, matching the other apply-to-all buttons. (Still undoable.) (July 2026)

v3.5 — Autosave now also captures the opacity and overlay view sliders (template, reference image, glyph) — previously a change to only those settings could be lost if the browser closed before another edit. (July 2026)

v3.6 — Accessibility polish. Keyboard focus now shows a clear gold outline on the letter tiles, step tabs, and buttons; the Hebrew letters in the grids are tagged as Hebrew so screen readers pronounce them with a Hebrew voice; and the on/off toggle buttons (dark mode, Default/Custom, Per Symbol/Combined, upper/lowercase, and the mark editor mode) now announce their pressed state to assistive technology. (July 2026)

v3.7 — Edit points by keyboard. In Edit-points mode you can now select points without a mouse: , and . step to the previous / next point, and i inserts a new point after the selected one — so the existing arrow-nudge and Delete shortcuts are finally reachable keyboard-only. (July 2026)

v3.8 — Crop from a sheet by keyboard. When cutting a letter or mark out of a "one image, all letters" / combined sheet, you can now do it without a mouse: the arrow keys move a crop box (Shift for smaller steps), + / − resize it, Enter crops, and Esc cancels. (July 2026)

v4.0 — Smarter tracing and a full point-editing suite. Tracing now picks a good ink threshold automatically, can even out photo lighting, and auto-detects every letter on a combined sheet for one-click review and assignment. Edit points grew into a real outline editor: delete whole contours or stray specks, snap to guides, copy/paste points between letters, flip / rotate / scale, a selection box with move & scale handles, marquee (M) and select-all, line ↔ curve segment switches, corner rounding with a live radius preview, a pen tool (P) that draws contours point by point — even on blank glyphs like digits — and a Contours panel with per-contour colors and hide-while-editing (hidden contours still export). Imported fonts round-trip faithfully: untouched glyphs keep their exact outlines, and hand edits never silently change a glyph's width. Plus a waterfall size preview on the Spacing step. (July 2026)

v4.1 — Auto-detect fixes. The detected-letter boxes now draw reliably in every browser — they were invisible in Firefox, which showed the sheet but not the gold boxes around each letter. And the ▦ Auto-detect letters button now sits right under the sheet, next to the page navigation, where you're already looking while boxing letters. (July 2026)

v4.10 — Cleaner UFO exports for font editors. The UFO source export no longer invents an x-height: Hebrew has no lowercase, so that guide was just a duplicate of the cap-height line and confused font editors like Glyphs and RoboFont. The field is now simply left unset, the honest answer for a caseless font. (July 2026)

v4.11 — More robust auto-detect review boxes. On the Auto-detect letters review screen, the outlined boxes around each detected letter now use fully self-contained sizing and styling, so they render consistently across browsers — a fix aimed at cases (notably Firefox) where the scanned sheet appeared but the boxes over it did not. (July 2026)

v4.12 — Auto-detect review boxes render reliably in Firefox. Following up on v4.11: the detected-letter outlines are now drawn as vector paths rather than rectangles, sidestepping a Firefox quirk that collapsed the rectangle outlines to zero size — so the boxes appear over the scanned sheet as intended, in every browser. (July 2026)

v4.14 — Auto-detect review boxes now appear in Firefox. The real culprit, finally pinned down: Firefox was hiding the entire box-overlay layer (it computed the interactive overlay group as display:none, unlike other browsers), so the detected-letter outlines and labels never showed even though the scanned sheet did. Forcing the overlay to display fixes it — the boxes now render in Firefox exactly as they do everywhere else. (July 2026)

v4.15 — Glyph-editor warnings match the rest of the app. A few notices in the custom-glyph editor — an invalid code point, a code point that's already taken, or converting a mark that has no shape yet — used a plain browser pop-up instead of the tool's own in-app dialog. They now use the same styled dialog as every other message, so the experience is consistent throughout. (July 2026)

v4.16 — Nikkud & trop editing controls moved beside the canvas. When you edit a vowel point or cantillation mark, its controls — the Simple editor / Upload image switch, the + Dot / + Bar buttons, the dot-size slider, and the shape toggle — now sit in the left panel next to the drawing area, instead of in a strip below it. That's the same spot the letter tools already use, so editing feels consistent, and it makes use of space that used to sit empty. (July 2026)

v4.17 — Clicking a nikkud or trop mark opens the full shape editor. Picking a vowel point or cantillation mark in its panel now opens the same Edit-shape window used on the letter-placement screen — dots & bars, its own undo, numeric size & position fields, and one-click Apply to all letters — instead of switching the whole workspace. Marks designed from an uploaded image (and combined-sheet mode) still go straight to their image tools. (July 2026)

v4.2 — A tidier Edit points panel. The point-editing controls are reorganized into clear zones: a sticky header with Done editing always in reach, a Select / Marquee / Pen mode switch, and a middle section that shows just the actions that apply to your current selection — with a Delete ▾ button that gathers point and contour deletion in one place. The Transform, Round corners, and Contours sections now look alike and remember whether you left them open. The long help paragraph became a short tip that changes with what you're doing, plus a ? button that jumps straight to the point-editing shortcuts — and the shortcuts sheet itself now covers every mouse trick too (double-click, Alt-click, segment dots, selection-box moves). Nothing about how editing works changed — every action, shortcut, and undo behaves exactly as before. (July 2026)

v4.3 — Sturdier exports. Your exported font now gets a valid internal name and download filename no matter what you call it — unusual family names (with slashes, brackets, %, emoji, accents, or Hebrew letters, or a name that's only spaces) used to produce a font some programs would reject or a file saved with no name; now they're always cleaned to a safe name (falling back to MyHebrewFont if nothing usable is left). And the font's version number only ticks up when an export actually finishes — a failed engine download no longer bumps it on every retry. (July 2026)

v4.4 — Your license always comes with your font. When you export a single TTF or WOFF2, the LICENSE.txt used to try to download by itself right after the font — which some browsers quietly block, leaving you with a font and no license. Now the Exported ✓ screen gives you a one-click ⬇ LICENSE.txt button (named after your font), so it can never be missed. The TTF + WOFF2 zip and UFO still bundle it inside as before. (July 2026)

v4.5 — A heads-up when a letter can't keep its curves. Once in a while a traced outline is too tangled for the font engine to turn its curves into the exact form a font file needs, so it quietly falls back to straight edges for that one letter — which used to happen with no warning, leaving a font that looked faceted with no clue why. Now the Exported ✓ screen tells you exactly which letters came out with straight edges, so you can re-trace or simplify just those and export again for smooth curves. Every other letter is unaffected. (July 2026)

v4.6 — Point editing gets a proper cockpit. Everything you use while pointing at the canvas now sits in a toolbar right above it: the Select / Marquee / Pen switch, Undo / Redo buttons (handy on a tablet), zoom, and three view toggles — Handles (show curve handles on every point, not just the selected ones), Guides (hide the guide lines while you look at a shape — snapping still works), and Snap. A slim status line under the canvas shows which letter you're editing, the live cursor position in font units, and how many points are selected, so the side panel is shorter and keeps just the actions for your selection. Your first time in, a one-line hint points the way (it retires itself after your first edit). Nothing about how editing works changed — every button, shortcut, and undo behaves exactly as before (the old hint line under the canvas is retired; the ? cheat sheet has every detail). (July 2026)

v4.7 — Two quiet export safeguards. First: if your project somehow carries a word spacing of zero (possible in very old or hand-edited save files — the slider itself never goes below 80), the exported font used to get a zero-width space, so every word ran together; the space now always exports at least the slider's minimum width. Second: when vowels or trop are enabled, every export runs a quick shaping check to confirm the marks actually position correctly — but if that checker couldn't load (say, a flaky connection), the font downloaded anyway with only a briefly-flashed note. Now the Exported ✓ screen tells you plainly when the check was skipped, so you know to test the font before sharing it. (July 2026)

v4.8 — Older projects export safely again. A project saved by a much older version (or edited outside the app) could be missing some of its vowel anchor points under the hood — and exporting it would fail with a generic "Export error" before your font ever built. The app now quietly restores any missing anchor points (in the same spots a fresh letter would get them) wherever it finds them — opening the anchor editor, previewing, or exporting — so those projects build normally; you can still fine-tune every anchor afterwards. (July 2026)

v4.9 — Your font's version number behaves itself. Two small bookkeeping fixes: a pre-1.0 version you typed yourself (like 0.5) no longer silently becomes 1.0-something in the exported file, and the automatic per-export version tick now only sticks when a font file actually downloads — cancelling after a failed shaping check, or a WOFF2 conversion hiccup, no longer inches the version up on every retry. (July 2026)

en: Anchoring — where the vowels go. "Anchoring" means showing the font where the vowel dots (nikkud) sit on each letter — and, if you want them, the cantillation marks (trop). Turn it on first: in the Nikkud (vowels) box on the left, tick Make my font Nikkud-compatible (and the same for Trop if you'd like). The 3 · Nikkud and 4 · Trop tabs then appear. Place the anchor: a handle appears on the letter — drag it to where the mark should sit. Choose which spot you're setting: Below — for most vowels, which sit under the letter. Above (Holam) — for the dot that sits on top. Dagesh (Center) — for the dot inside the letter. Tap the vowel buttons to preview different vowels in place, and use Nikkud size to scale all the marks up or down. Your moves apply live and travel with you to the next letter — when one looks right, click ✓ Confirm placement to mark it reviewed (its dot turns a solid green ✓). Confirming is optional; undo always works. Reset letter or Reset all let you start over. 💡 For tiny adjustments, drag the handle and use your arrow keys (hold Shift for extra-fine moves), or type exact X / Y values on the right. Do this for every letter so vowels line up neatly when people type.

Exporting & installing your font. When your letters are ready, choose a format in the picker next to ⬇ Export TTF (top-right), then click the button. It builds a real font from your work. Which format? TTF (recommended) — a normal font file to install and type with in Word, Google Docs, Canva — anywhere you choose fonts. Start here. WOFF2 (web) — a compressed font for embedding on a website. TTF + WOFF2 (zip) — both files plus a ready-to-paste @font-face CSS snippet. UFO source (zip) — an editable source for font editors (FontForge, Glyphs, RoboFont), with real curves, anchors and a features.fea. Every export comes with a LICENSE.txt — the license you picked in Font Details, with your name as author. The TTF + WOFF2 zip and the UFO keep it inside the download; a single TTF or WOFF2 offers it as a one-click ⬇ LICENSE.txt button on the Exported ✓ screen. Install the TTF: Mac: double-click the .ttf file, then click Install Font. Windows: right-click the .ttf file and choose Install. Then pick your font by name wherever you choose fonts. 💡 The very first export downloads a one-time font engine (about 8 MB), so give it a moment — after that it's quick. Check it & share it. The 🔍 QA Check button scans every letter–mark pair for collisions (see the QA Check tab), and ★ Use this Font in IvritSuite — the last item in the format picker — lets you read with your font right inside any IvritSuite tool (see the Use in IvritSuite tab). Preview PDF. The Preview PDF button (top bar) makes a printable specimen sheet — a cover page plus a chart of every letter paired with each vowel. A great way to proofread your whole font on one page before you install it. Made changes and re-exporting? The version number ticks up automatically each time. If you'd already installed an older copy, delete it first so your computer picks up the new one. (If some letters aren't traced or anchored yet, the tool warns you — those letters would come out blank.)

Use this font in IvritSuite. You can read with your own font right inside any IvritSuite tool's font picker — without installing anything on your computer. Save it: choose ★ Use this Font in IvritSuite at the bottom of the export format picker and click the button — or, after any normal export, say yes to the “Save to My Fonts?” prompt. Your font is stored in this browser. Manage them: the My IvritSuite Fonts window lists everything you've saved, each with buttons to download or remove it. Keep up to 10 — saving an 11th drops the oldest. Use it: open any IvritSuite tool (e.g. Torah Trainer) in this same browser, open its font picker, and pick your font under My Fonts. Your letters, vowels and trop all render using the anchors you set here. ⚠️ Saved fonts live on this browser, on this device — this isn't a cloud account. To use a font on another computer, export the TTF and save it there too. Clearing your browser data removes saved fonts.

Choosing a license. Your license tells the world what others may do with your font. Pick one in the Font Details box — it's written into the font and into the LICENSE.txt that downloads with your export. They're listed from most open to most strict: Public Domain (CC0) — you give up all rights; anyone can use, change, sell, or share it freely, no credit needed. The most generous option. SIL Open Font License 1.1 (OFL) — the standard for free fonts: anyone may use, study, modify, and share it (even bundled in paid software), but it can't be sold on its own and must stay under the OFL. MIT — very permissive: do almost anything, just keep the copyright + permission notice. All Rights Reserved — fully proprietary: nobody may use, copy, or modify it without your written permission. The most restrictive. 💛 If you can, choose a more open license (CC0, OFL, or MIT). Open Hebrew fonts are a real gift for students, teachers, and anyone learning to read — they make your work usable in classrooms, siddurim, and projects you'll never even see. ⚠️ Every license generated here includes a Made with IvritSuite.com attribution line. This line must stay in the LICENSE file — it's what keeps the tool free for everyone.

QA Check — catch collisions before you export. Click 🔍 QA Check (top bar) to open a grid showing every letter paired with every vowel and trop mark. It reads your font silently — it never changes anything. Red cells flag a real ink collision worth a look: a mark sitting on top of the letter's ink (overlapping it), or a below mark running into a letter's descender tail — the part that hangs below the line, like ך or ק. To fix one, go back to the 3 · Nikkud or 4 · Trop step for that letter and nudge its anchor (or shrink Nikkud size), then re-check. 💡 A note at the top warns when a tall mark or letter will expand the font's vertical box — that's expected and exports fine; it just means the font grew a little taller. And not every red cell is a disaster: glance at each and trust your eye.

en: Saving your project. Your project is your work-in-progress — all your images, outlines, anchors and settings. Save it so you can come back and keep editing later. Save Project (top bar) gives you two choices. To computer downloads a single .hebrewfont file with everything packed inside — your permanent backup. In this browser keeps a quick copy on this device that you can reopen any time from Load Project ▾ → Recent. Load Project ▾ reopens a saved .hebrewfont file from your computer, or a recent in-browser save. ⚠️ This is your editable project, not the font itself. To get a font you can install and type with, see the Exporting & Installing tab. The browser copy (and the automatic safety-net save) is handy, but it is not a real backup — if you clear your browser data or switch computers, it's gone. Save “To computer” regularly to keep a file you can't lose.

Share your font. Made a font you're proud of? Open Hebrew fonts are a real gift to teachers, students, and siddur-makers. Here are good places to share yours. ⚠️ Wherever you share, include your LICENSE.txt (every export provides one — inside the zip/UFO, or via the ⬇ LICENSE.txt button for a single TTF/WOFF2). Most platforms below require an open license such as the SIL Open Font License (OFL) — set one in the Font Details box and re-export if needed. Google Fonts — the largest home for free fonts; once accepted, anyone can use yours on the web (OFL required). See the submission guide and onboarding docs. Open Siddur — Hebrew font pack — a curated, open-source Unicode Hebrew font collection for liturgical and educational use: opensiddur.org/help/fonts. The Open Font Library — upload and share libre fonts directly: fontlibrary.org. The Culmus Project — the long-running home of free Hebrew fonts: github.com/Culmus. Alef Alef Alef (אלף אלף אלף) — Israel's community library of free, libre Hebrew fonts; browse the collection and share your own: alefalefalef.co.il. GitHub — publish your font and its license in a public repo so others can find and improve it (also the usual first step toward Google Fonts). Add it to IvritSuite. I'd love to feature your font in the IvritSuite font library. To submit it, use the 📤 Share this font button on the export-success screen — or the ✚ Submit a font button on the Resources → Fonts page. Either one opens a pre-filled submission email to Harrison@IvritSuite.com. Fill in or confirm these details, then attach your files: Font name and type — Block / Cursive / Torah / Other. Whether it supports nikkud and trop. Its license (CC0 / OFL / MIT / Other) and version. Your name and website (optional). 📎 Attach the exported font file (TTF / OTF / WOFF) and its LICENSE.txt — the zip/UFO already include it; for a single TTF/WOFF2, grab the ⬇ LICENSE.txt button on the Exported ✓ screen. 💛 Open licenses (CC0, OFL, MIT) let your font reach classrooms, siddurim, and projects you'll never even see. If you can, share it freely.

en: Spacing. Open the Spacing panel on the left to control the gaps in your finished font. A live preview updates as you slide: Letter spacing — the gap between letters. Word spacing — the width of the space between words. Line spacing — the gap between lines of text. Kerning — fine-tune the gap for specific letter pairs that need it (some combinations look too tight or too loose at the default spacing). Pick the two sides, set the gap, and click Add pair — it's saved as real OpenType kerning and shows in the preview. Sample text — type any Hebrew here to see how it looks. Reset spacing puts everything back to the defaults. 💡 The preview uses your traced letters. Any letter you haven't traced yet shows up as a dashed box — that's just a placeholder, not part of your font.

Welcome 👋 Hebrew Font Maker turns your hand-drawn Hebrew letters into a real font you can install on your computer and type with — vowels (nikkud) and cantillation marks (trop) included. ▶ Take a tour · ⌨ Keyboard shortcuts. Here's the whole journey, start to finish: Upload a clear picture of each letter. Trace — the tool turns each picture into a clean outline. Anchor — show where the vowel dots sit on each letter. Spacing — fine-tune the gaps between letters and words. Export & install — download your finished font and use it anywhere. Use the tabs above to read about each step. You can work through them roughly in order, one letter at a time. Before you start, give your font a name in the Font Details box (top-left). The Family name is what you'll see in font menus later. The version number takes care of itself. 💡 Works best on a desktop or laptop. Your work is auto-saved in this browser as you go, but use Save Project for a real backup you can keep (see the Saving tab). Made a mistake? Undo / Redo — the ↶ ↷ buttons in the top bar, or Ctrl/⌘-Z and Ctrl/⌘-Shift-Z — step back and forth through your edits. Press ? anytime for the full list of keyboard shortcuts.

Printable handwriting templates. Prefer to write on paper? Print one of these worksheets, fill the boxes with your own Hebrew, then scan or photograph the page and bring it back in here to build your font. How it works: Print a template below at actual size (100% — turn "Fit to page" off), on plain white paper. Write one glyph or mark per box, in dark ink. The small blue label in each corner shows what goes there — a reference glyph, its name, and its U+ code. For vowels and trop it also says below / above / center so you know where the mark sits on the letter. Scan at 300 DPI or higher (or take a straight-on, evenly-lit photo with no shadows). Save it as a PNG or a high-quality JPG. Import it on the Uploading step: choose One image with all letters, then drag a box around each glyph to cut it out. 💡 The grid prints in light blue on purpose: the tracer only keeps dark ink, so the blue boxes and labels disappear by themselves — just keep your writing dark and inside each box. (Keep the Ink threshold near its default; pushing it much higher can start to pick up the light grid.) ✍️ A black or dark-blue felt-tip or fineliner reads far better than pencil or a light ballpoint. Write boldly and fill the box. Download a template — PDF to print, or Picture for an image file. ⚠️ The Letters and English Letters sheets are two pages each — each downloads as a 2-page PDF, or as two numbered images (…_1.png, …_2.png) when you choose Picture.

Tracing. Tracing turns your photo into a smooth outline the font can actually use. Open the 2 · Trace tab — the first time, it traces automatically. If it doesn't look right, nudge these: Ink threshold — how dark a spot has to be to count as ink. Slide it down if light strokes are being missed, or up if the paper/background is bleeding in. Detail (less ↔ more) — slide left for a smoother, cleaner outline; right to hug every little bump of your handwriting. Invert (light ink on dark) — turn this on if you wrote in white or light ink on a dark background. Click Re-trace to redo it with your new settings, or Clear to start the letter over. The dot turns blue once a letter is traced. Fine-tune the outline by hand. Once a letter is traced, click ✎ Edit points to tidy the shape: drag any point to move it, nudge the selected point with the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger steps), or press Delete to remove it. Click Done editing when it looks right. 💡 The holes inside letters like ס, ם and ע are found and punched out for you automatically.

en: Uploading your letters. You'll bring in a picture of each of the 27 Hebrew letters. Clear dark ink on white paper works best. Pick how you want to add them in the Add Letters panel on the left: One letter per image — upload one photo per letter. Simplest if you're scanning or photographing letters one at a time. One image with all letters — upload one photo of a whole sheet of letters, then pick a letter and drag a box around it to cut it out. Existing font file — already have a font file? Import it and the letters come in ready-made, so you can skip tracing entirely. Allowed files: any image — PNG, JPG, GIF or WebP. Transparent PNGs and letters drawn on a plain white background also work great. (For the Existing font file option, a TTF or OTF font file.) ✒️ Have vector artwork? Turn on Enable SVG uploading under Advanced Settings → Input mode to drop in SVG files — their vector paths become the glyph outlines directly, with no tracing. See the SVG Upload Guide there for naming one sheet so its letters auto-split. Tracing guide: a faint reference letter shows behind yours so you can line things up. On the right of the canvas, dial the Reference letter opacity slider (or untick Show reference glyph behind to hide it), and use Imported image opacity to fade your own photo in or out. Position it (the 1 · Align step): click a letter in the grid on the left, then use the adjustment buttons on the left of the canvas — Wider, Taller, Rotate, Skew — to sit your letter neatly on the guide lines. The little dot on that letter turns orange once it has an image. 🖨️ Don't have letters to scan yet? The Download Templates tab gives you printable sheets — handwrite each letter in the boxes, scan or photograph the page, then bring it in here with One image with all letters.

Tips: group transforms are honored, so flatten/ungroup freely; convert strokes to fills first (open strokes don't fill); clipped, masked, hidden, and <use>-referenced elements are skipped.

IvritSuite is designed to be safely usable by students of all ages, including children under 13. The site does not knowingly collect personal information from any user, regardless of age. There is no account creation, no submission form, no chat, and no upload feature. If you believe any personal information has somehow been collected in violation of this policy, please contact us through the contact page and we will remove it.

IvritSuite is almost entirely client-side. There are no accounts, no logins, and no submissions, and the site stores no personal data on a server. Specifically: No personal information. The site does not ask for, transmit, or store your name, email address, school, classroom roster, or any other personally identifiable information. Tool content stays in your browser. Anything you create with the tools — worksheet presets, classroom-dashboard schedules and settings, flash-card preferences, dictionary filters, Torah Trainer settings — is stored locally in your browser using the standard localStorage API. It never leaves your device through any channel operated by the site. No tracking pixels or fingerprinting. For aggregate usage statistics the site uses only Google Analytics 4, described in Section 3.
Questions or concerns about this policy can be directed to Harrison Bleiberg via the contact page, or by email at {email}.

The site uses Google Analytics 4 (measurement ID G-CMLC81Z0HC) to understand which tools are used and how visitors arrive at the site. GA4 collects aggregated, anonymized data such as page views, approximate geographic region, device class, and referral source. IP addresses are anonymized by GA4 by default and are not stored by the site operator. You can control or block analytics in several ways: Use your browser's "Do Not Track" or tracking-protection settings. Install the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on. Block third-party scripts via your preferred ad/tracker blocker. For details on Google's data handling, see Google's Privacy Policy.

The site's only data collection is anonymized, aggregated Google Analytics 4 usage data (page views, device class, region). GA4 anonymizes IP addresses and is not associated with any student identifier; this data is not directly or indirectly linkable to individual students and therefore does not constitute "education records" or "personally identifiable information" under 34 CFR § 99.3.

Because no PII or education records are disclosed to the site, schools and districts may permit teachers and students to use IvritSuite without entering into a separate data-sharing or "school official" agreement under the FERPA exception at 34 CFR § 99.31(a)(1). If your district nevertheless requires a written acknowledgment of these practices, you may rely on this policy as a public statement of them.

This section is provided for school administrators, IT departments, and educators evaluating IvritSuite for classroom use under the U.S. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA, 20 U.S.C. § 1232g; 34 CFR Part 99).
IvritSuite does not sell, rent, license, or otherwise share any user information with advertisers or data brokers. The site displays no advertising.

IvritSuite does not collect, receive, store, or transmit any personally identifiable information (PII) from student education records as defined by FERPA. The site has no user accounts, no class rosters, no grade books, no submission of student work, and no server-side storage of teacher- or student-generated content. Worksheets, presets, schedules, and tool preferences are stored exclusively in the local browser using localStorage and remain on the user's own device.

Because no student records are stored by the site, there is nothing for parents to inspect, amend, or have removed under FERPA's parental-rights provisions on the site's side. Parents wishing to review locally stored tool settings can do so directly in the browser used by the student via the home-page Import / Export All Settings control.
For FERPA-specific inquiries, please contact Harrison Bleiberg through the contact page.

IvritSuite (the "site") is a free collection of Hebrew literacy tools for teachers and students, operated by Harrison Bleiberg. This Privacy Policy explains what information the site collects (and, more importantly, what it does not), how that information is used, and the choices you have. By using the site you agree to the practices described here.

Because all of your settings live only in your browser, you have full control: The Import / Export All Settings button on the home page lets you download a single JSON backup of every tool's data, restore from a backup, or erase everything in one click. Clearing your browser's site data for IvritSuite removes all stored settings and presets. Using a different browser, device, or private/incognito window will give you a fresh, separate set of settings.

The site is delivered over HTTPS. Because no user data is transmitted to a server operated by the site, the primary security boundary is the user's own browser and device. We recommend keeping your browser up to date and using device-level protections appropriate to your setting.

Some tools fetch or link to third-party content. Visiting or interacting with these resources is governed by their own privacy policies, not by IvritSuite: Kaikki.org — source of the Hebrew word data used in the dictionary and worksheet generator. PocketTorah — chanted-audio source used by the Torah Trainer. Google Fonts — Hebrew and Latin web fonts. Public weather APIs used by the Classroom Dashboard to display current local weather (only the location you enter is sent, in the standard form required to look up a forecast). Web3Forms and hCaptcha — used only if you send a message through the contact page or the "Suggest a Resource" form on the resources page. The information you enter in those forms is passed to Web3Forms solely to deliver the email to the site operator, and the form uses hCaptcha to block automated spam; both process that data under their own privacy policies. Nothing from the form is stored by IvritSuite.

A free interactive tutor for the Torah cantillation marks. Learn mode teaches each mark's symbol, names, and melody with real chanted examples; Drill mode quizzes you three ways with per-mark mastery tracking.

Cantillation marks printed above and below the words of the Hebrew Bible. Each mark names a melodic phrase and marks the grammar of the verse — together they tell you how to chant it.

Each session asks 10 questions of three kinds: name the trope on a marked word, pick the symbol for a melody you hear, or pick the melody that matches a symbol. Marks you miss come up more often, and distractors get sneakier (pashta vs. kadma) as your mastery grows.

Learn the Torah cantillation marks — names, symbols, and melodies — with real chanted examples.
Ornamental short phrases: kadma-v'azla (geresh), double gershayim, the telisha twins at the word's edges, and the whirling pazer.
The workhorse mid-verse clause: mahpach and pashta climb toward zakef katon's little pause. Pashta looks exactly like kadma — only its position at the end of the word gives it away.
Once-in-a-Torah specialties — mercha kefula, karnei parah, and yerach ben yomo. Karnei parah and yerach ben yomo each appear exactly once, back to back, in Numbers 35:5.
Gentler pauses: revia hovers above the word like a single gem, while darga and tevir often pair up in a distinctive stair-step figure.
A grand early pause in long verses: zarka swings up and hands off to segol. Shalshelet — a rare, dramatic chain of notes — stands in for it at the very start of a verse.
Home base: the backbone of every verse. Mercha and tipcha lead into etnachta — the deep mid-verse resting point — and the same team walks the second half down to the final sof pasuk cadence.

Sits on the stressed syllable, usually leading straight into a geresh ("kadma v'azla"). Same shape as pashta, which instead hangs off the word's end.

Postpositive — printed at the very end of the word even when the stress falls earlier (it's doubled on the stress in that case). Same shape as kadma; position tells them apart.
Postpositive — the three-dot cluster rides off the end of the word.
A long, dramatic chain of notes — always on a verse's first word, always followed by a vertical paseq line.
The verse-ending cadence. Its siluk mark shares a codepoint with the meteg stress line, so learn it by position: the last word of every verse, followed by the ׃ mark.
Prepositive — the small circle leads the word from the front.
Postpositive — the small circle sits at the end of the word.
"Moon one day old" — appears once in the Torah, right before karnei parah's word (Numbers 35:5).
Prepositive — printed at the very start of the word, below the first letter. Same shape as mahpach, different position and role.
Zakef katon's louder sibling — a vertical bar joins the two dots when the word stands alone in its clause.
Postpositive — curls off the end of the word and always throws ahead to a segol.
